en_US.title: Worker Locker Seal Failure
en_US.scanner: WORKER LOCKER // Seal folded inward. External pressure breach. Meal tin, suit patch, and tool tag still inside.
en_US.codex: The locker was not looted before the flood. Its seal folded inward from outside pressure, pinning the door against a meal tin, a patched suit layer, and a Barnard-cut tool tag left on the inner hook. The room failed around the worker's day, not after it had been cleaned.
en_US.pda_log: Locker row note: inward seal failure; contents present; no pry marks; tool tag retained. Hold salvage count until custody path is established.
en_US.environmental_label: WORKER LOCKER // INWARD SEAL FAILURE // CONTENTS PRESENT
en_US.in_game_wiki: This locker is an early worker-room evidence object. It teaches damage direction before accusation: outside pressure entered first, the worker's belongings remained in place, and no one had time to strip the row for orderly salvage.
en_US.external_site: A drowned worker locker on HECTON-8 preserves the moment pressure entered the room before people, tools, or food could be cleared.
en_US.external_site_article: The worker locker is a small object with a hard timeline. Its seal folded inward, which means outside pressure entered the room before anyone opened the door from within. The meal tin, patched suit layer, and tool tag stayed where a worker left them. That matters because the room reads as evidence, not scenery: the flood interrupted a shift, not an abandoned storage sweep. For the player, the first human truth is physical, readable, and quiet.

en_US.codex: The mess heater failed after water crossed the coil housing. A lunch token remains clipped to the serving rail, unspent, with its credit strip swollen under salt. The room kept a meal waiting longer than the people could.

en_US.in_game_wiki: The mess heater makes the drowned worker room feel used. It ties food, heat, wage credit, and salvage into one object: a meal paid for, never claimed, and still physically clipped to the rail.
en_US.external_site: A failed mess heater in HECTON-8 preserves an unspent lunch token, turning worker-room food service into evidence of interrupted life.
en_US.external_site_article: The lunch token is useful because it is petty. It is not a grand memorial, only a cheap credit marker still clipped to a rail beside a dead heater coil. Water crossed the housing before the meal could be pulled. Salt swelled the strip, but the token stayed put. In a salvage game, that tiny unpaid lunch matters: it proves the colony was not only machines and contracts. It was shifts, hunger, credit, waiting, and a room that failed before a worker came back.

en_US.codex: The mark is small enough to miss under salt bloom: Barnard Yards, second-grade alloy, old pressure-die cut. Its grip has two repair pins and a worker-made shim. Deep Reach did not issue the tool; someone brought older, trusted metal down to the moon.

en_US.external_site_article: The Barnard tool mark is not a family revelation or a heroic relic. It is a cheap alloy stamp almost hidden under salt. That restraint is the point.
